“I learned from a peddler who, while traveling through your part of the country this winter, had a tooth pulled, that Bovary was still working hard. That does not surprise me, and he showed me his tooth; we had coffee together. I asked him whether he had seen you; he told me he had not, but that he had seen two animals in the stable, from which I conclude that business is going well. So much the better, my dear children, and may the good Lord send you every imaginable happiness.

“It grieves me that I still do not know my beloved little granddaughter Berthe Bovary. I have planted an oat-plum tree for her in the garden, beneath your room, and I do not want anyone to touch it, except to make preserves for her later, which I shall keep in the cupboard for her, when she comes.

“Farewell, my dear children. I embrace you, my daughter; you too, my son-in-law, and the little one, on both cheeks.

“I remain, with many compliments,

“Your affectionate father,

“THEODORE ROUAULT.”

For several minutes she remained holding the thick paper between her fingers. The spelling mistakes intertwined with one another, and Emma followed the sweet thought that chattered all through it like a hen half hidden in a thorn hedge. The writing had been dried with ashes from the hearth, for a little gray dust slipped from the letter onto her dress, and she almost thought she could see her father bending toward the fireplace to take up the tongs. How long it had been since she had sat beside him, on the footstool, in the chimney corner, when she would burn the end of a stick in the tall flame of the crackling sea rushes!...

She remembered summer evenings filled with sunlight. The foals neighed when anyone passed and galloped, galloped... Beneath her window there was a beehive, and sometimes the bees, wheeling in the light, struck the windowpanes like rebounding balls of gold. What happiness there had been then! What freedom! What hope! What an abundance of illusions! None remained now! She had spent them on all the adventures of her soul, through all her successive states, in virginity, in marriage, and in love—thus losing them continually throughout her life, like a traveler who leaves some of his wealth at every inn along the road.

But what, then, was making her so unhappy? Where was the extraordinary catastrophe that had devastated her? And she raised her head, looking around her as though searching for the cause of what was making her suffer.

A ray of April light shimmered on the porcelain on the shelf; the fire was burning; beneath her slippers she felt the softness of the carpet; the daylight was white, the air warm, and she heard her child bursting into peals of laughter.

Indeed, the little girl was then rolling about on the lawn, amid the grass that was being turned for hay. She was lying flat on her stomach at the top of a haystack. Her nurse was holding her by the skirt. Lestiboudois was raking nearby, and every time he came close, she leaned over, beating the air with both arms.

“Bring her to me!” said her mother, rushing forward to embrace her. “How I love you, my poor child! How I love you!”

Then, noticing that the tips of her ears were a little dirty, she quickly rang for hot water and cleaned her, changed her underclothes, stockings, and shoes, asked a thousand questions about her health, as though she had just returned from a journey, and finally, kissing her again and shedding a few tears, she handed her back to the servant, who remained utterly astonished at this excess of tenderness.

That evening, Rodolphe found her more serious than usual.

“It will pass,” he decided. “It is a whim.”

And he failed to keep three appointments in succession. When he returned, she was cold and almost disdainful toward him.

“Ah! You are wasting your time, my pretty one...”

And he appeared not to notice either her melancholy sighs or the handkerchief she was pulling out.

It was then that Emma repented!

She even wondered why she detested Charles, and whether it would not have been better if she could have loved him. But he offered little purchase for such revivals of feeling, so that she remained greatly perplexed in her half-formed impulse toward sacrifice, when the apothecary happened to provide her with an opportunity.




XI


He had recently read a eulogy of a new method for curing clubfeet; and as he was a supporter of progress, he conceived the patriotic idea that Yonville, in order to keep abreast, ought to have operations for strephopodia.

“For,” he said to Emma, “what is there to risk? Consider”—and he counted the advantages of the attempt on his fingers—“almost certain success, relief and improved appearance for the patient, fame quickly acquired by the operator. Why, for example, should your husband not wish to rid poor Hippolyte, from the Golden Lion, of his affliction? Bear in mind that he would not fail to tell all the travelers about his cure, and then”—Homais lowered his voice and looked around him—“who could prevent me from sending a short notice about it to the newspaper? Good Lord! An article circulates... people talk about it... it ends by snowballing! And who knows? Who knows?”

Indeed, Bovary might succeed; nothing assured Emma that he was not skillful, and what satisfaction it would be for her to have encouraged him to take a step by which his reputation and fortune would be increased! All she asked was to lean on something more solid than love.

Urged by the apothecary and by her, Charles allowed himself to be persuaded. He sent to Rouen for Doctor Duval’s volume, and every evening, his head in his hands, he immersed himself in his reading.

While he studied equinus, varus, and valgus—that is, strephocatopodia, strephendopodia, and strephexopodia (or, to put it more clearly, the different deviations of the foot, whether downward, inward, or outward)—together with strephyopodia and strephanopodia (in other words, twisting underneath and straightening upward), Monsieur Homais, with all manner of arguments, exhorted the inn servant to submit to the operation.

“You will perhaps feel scarcely more than a slight pain; it is merely a prick, like a minor bloodletting, less than the removal of certain corns.”
